analysis.one_liner: Restructures Medicare around private-plan competition, raises the eligibility age, and adds tax-advantaged health savings accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and no vote, three weeks before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have folded Medicare's hospital and doctor coverage into a single program run through competitive bidding among private plans, raised the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 67 and then indexed it upward with life expectancy, and banned new enrollment in medigap supplemental policies. It would have created a new annual out-of-pocket cap for beneficiaries and replaced the separate hospital and doctor deductibles with one lower deductible, while also creating mandatory tax-deductible 'health individual retirement accounts' and cutting the Medicare payroll tax for workers past 65.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Advantage insurers would gain a much larger permanent role: every private plan would have to include drug coverage, medigap would be closed to new enrollees, and every region would need at least two private plans per coverage tier. Financial firms would gain a new stream of tax-advantaged accounts. Higher-income workers would gain from payroll-tax elimination at 67 and tax-deductible savings contributions. Some seniors would gain an annual out-of-pocket cap and a single lower deductible.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage insurers and high earners

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the separate Part A hospital deductible and Part B deductible with one unified deductible ($550 in 2016), which is lower than the hospital deductible then in effect.

Adds an annual limit on out-of-pocket deductibles and coinsurance, tied to the IRS limit for high-deductible health plans — traditional Medicare has never had such a cap, so a beneficiary with a catastrophic illness would stop paying cost-sharing at that point.
Cuts the Medicare hospital insurance payroll tax by 50% at age 65 and eliminates it entirely at 67, to encourage later retirement.
Repeals the Independent Payment Advisory Board and the Medicare payment productivity adjustments after 2020, and freezes the 2013 physician payment update at zero.
Ends late-enrollment penalties for any month a person had other health coverage, and gives current part-B-only or part-A-only enrollees a special enrollment without penalties.
Deposits a per-capita preventive-benefit amount into the health savings account of each fee-for-service enrollee each year.

analysis.who_pays: Future 65- to 66-year-olds would face a longer wait for Medicare, with earlier enrollment available only at premiums set so that early enrollees pay actuarially for it. Beneficiaries would bear more premium risk as competitive bidding capped the federal payment at a share of regional bids, including a bid from the traditional program itself. People who could not save $2,500 a year would get little from the new accounts, while the tax deductions for them compound with income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Near-retirees facing a longer wait for Medicare

drawbacks.text: The bill defines a 'preferred Medicare age' that rises to 67 by 2025 and thereafter increases with life expectancy, so future retirees would wait longer than 65 for Medicare; they could enroll earlier only at premiums calculated so early and late enrollees come out actuarially equal.

New enrollment in medigap supplemental policies would be banned after the effective date; only current policyholders could keep or switch their coverage, pushing new seniors into the bill's tiered private plans.

Competitive bidding would set the federal benchmark at roughly 88% of regional bids, and the traditional fee-for-service program would itself have to bid — a structure in which health costs growing faster than bids show up as higher premiums for beneficiaries.

Mandatory HIRA contributions of $2,500 per person ($5,000 per couple) would be excluded from taxable income and earn a refundable saver's credit — a benefit that scales with income — while the Medicare payroll tax is eliminated for workers at 67.

Low-income dual-eligible beneficiaries would be auto-enrolled in Medicare Advantage managed care or shifted into state-financed accounts, and Medicaid would no longer cover services Medicare could pay for, with states required to pick from specified maintenance-of-effort options.
Distributions from the new accounts could not be used for abortion or euthanasia, and the bill adds conscience protections allowing providers to refuse such services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine beneficiary protections — a real annual out-of-pocket cap and one lower unified deductible — are meaningful, and traditional Medicare's lack of a catastrophic limit is a true weakness the bill addresses. But those gains sit on top of a structure that raises the eligibility age past 67, caps federal payments through bidding that shifts cost-growth risk onto premiums, eliminates medigap for new enrollees, and channels tax benefits through accounts that mainly help people who can already save. The bill asks future near-retirees and plan enrollees to bear the financing risk while insurers gain a permanently larger, protected role.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with three weeks left in the session and not a single cosponsor, it was referred to three committees and then a subcommittee, and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wally Herger introduced the bill on December 11, 2012, three weeks before the 112th Congress expired.
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Rules Committees on the day of introduction, and to the Health Subcommittee on December 19, 2012.
No member joined as a cosponsor.
No committee or subcommittee ever acted further, and no vote of any kind was held before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency gained. The Medicare program, its financing rules, Medicare Advantage insurers, and the tax code were all left exactly as they were; the bill was a proposal that died on arrival, not a change anyone had to absorb.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, and the Republican sponsor attracted zero cosponsors — not even from his own party — so no partisan or bipartisan pattern of support ever formed.

industries.note: The bill makes every Medicare Advantage plan include drug coverage, replaces medigap for new seniors with three tiers of private plans, and requires at least two private plans per tier in every region — making private insurers the permanent channel through which Medicare dollars flow. Beneficiaries get catastrophic protection in exchange, but the industry's revenue role is locked in regardless of how the plans perform.

New enrollment in supplemental policies would be banned after the effective date, with current policyholders grandfathered. The bill's case is that medigap first-dollar coverage drives up Medicare costs; current enrollees lose the option they chose, and the bill directs new seniors toward private plans instead.

The bill creates a tax-exempt Health Individual Retirement Account Fund, mandatory tax-deductible contributions of up to $2,500 per person per year, and a refundable saver's credit — a new pool of tax-advantaged money and fees. The tax deductions benefit most those with income high enough to save at those levels.

Wealthier workers gain the payroll-tax elimination at 67 and the HIRA deductions, but lose because the bill reduces the government's premium contribution for high-income seniors. The tax-side gains outweigh the subsidy loss for those with high earnings.

Physicians would face a one-year payment freeze in 2013, but the repeal of productivity adjustments after 2020 raises payment growth, and a new graduate medical education grant program and trust fund would replace current GME financing.
